result.summary: Turnus tries to burn the Trojan fleet, but Cybele saves the ships by turning them into sea nymphs. After Turnus falls and Ardea burns, a bird rises from the ashes, and Venus wins Jupiter's consent to make Æneas a god, which the river Numicius and Venus then bring about.

scenes.title: Cybele saves the burning ships
scenes.summary: Turnus fires the Trojan ships; Cybele raises a storm, frees the ships and turns them into sea Naiads who still help sailors except Greeks.
scenes.stakes: The Trojan fleet, made of Cybele's sacred pines, faces destruction by fire.

scenes.title: Turnus falls; Ardea burns
scenes.summary: Turnus persists in the war; Æneas wins, Turnus dies, and Ardea is burnt, and a bird rises from its ruins.
scenes.stakes: Turnus and his city face defeat and destruction.

scenes.title: Venus pleads with Jupiter
scenes.summary: Venus begs Jupiter to make Æneas a god; the gods and Juno assent and Jupiter grants it.
scenes.stakes: Æneas's chance at immortality depends on Jupiter's consent.

scenes.title: Æneas becomes a god
scenes.summary: Venus has the river Numicius wash away Æneas's mortal part, anoints him with ambrosia and nectar, and the Romans worship him as Indiges.

alias_notes.explanation: Epithet of Venus, linked to the island Cythera.
Title given to Æneas as a deified native god.

notable_quotes.reason: Shows the war continuing from pride and shame rather than any real aim.

analysis.text: Divine protection and transformation save Troy's remnant, linking Ovid's metamorphoses to Rome's founding.
Æneas's apotheosis as Indiges echoes Roman cult and prepares for the deification of rulers such as Julius Caesar and Augustus.

legacy.text: The ships-to-nymphs episode comes from Virgil's Aeneid, which Ovid reworks, and the Ardea bird (heron) gives a Latin pun on the name.

fun_facts.text: Ardea means heron in Latin, so the bird from the ashes is a pun on the city's name.

language_notes.text: The Ætolian arms refused: Turnus's envoy had sought help from Diomedes, a Greek hero now settled in Italy, who declined to fight the Trojans.
The Mother of the Gods is Cybele, whose sacred pines on Mount Ida were felled to build the Trojan ships; cymbals and pipes belong to her rites.
Sons of Astræus are the winds, brothers born of the Titan Astræus; Cybele borrows one to break the ships' moorings.
'Him of Neritos' is Ulysses, from Ithaca's Mount Neritos; the Pelasgians are the Greeks. His ship's wreck is not shown here but alluded to.
Alcinoüs's ship refers to the Phaeacian ship that carried Ulysses home and was turned to stone by Neptune near the coast.
"Prodigy" means a portent or marvel; here the transformation of Æneas's ships into sea Nymphs.
Lavinia, daughter of King Latinus, was the prize promised to Æneas; Turnus had also sought her hand, which was the original cause of the war.
Ardea was Turnus's city; its name suggests Latin ardea, 'heron', which prepares for the bird that rises from the ashes.
Iülus is Ascanius, son of Æneas; Cytherea is Venus, named for the island of Cythera, associated with her.
The "unsightly realms" and Stygian streams refer to the underworld, which Æneas had already visited alive.
Numicius is a small river in Latium near Laurentum; here a river god with reeds and horns.
"People of Quirinus" means the Romans, after Romulus deified as Quirinus. Indiges is a title for a deified native hero or local god.

context_notes.text: Cybele's lions drew her chariot; she was a Phrygian mother goddess, so she protects the Trojan (Phrygian) fleet built from her sacred trees.
Naiads are properly freshwater nymphs; here the ships become sea nymphs, a new kind of divine being in the ocean.
Both sides have divine backing: Venus and later Juno's reluctant stance for the Trojans, and local gods for the Rutulians.
Juno, the royal wife of Jupiter, had long persecuted the Trojans, so her assent marks the end of her hostility.
Doves were the birds that drew Venus's chariot.
Ambrosia and nectar were the food and drink of the gods, conferring immortality.

literary_notes.text: Ships that survived the sea now fear fire, a reversal of the danger they had escaped.
Each ship part is matched to a body part, so the transformation is told as a point-by-point correspondence between hull and body.
The nymphs keep human memory and loyalties, helping sailors but shunning Greeks, so the transformation preserves Trojan feeling.
The narrator turns to address Lavinia directly, adding pathos by showing she is no longer even the aim of the fighting.
The bird takes on the city's voice, pallor and mourning, so the ruined city seems to lament itself.
The repeated "enough" and "once" make Venus's plea sound modest and persuasive.
The surviving "superior essence" signifies the divine part of Æneas, separated from mortality by apotheosis.
